title: Arcing faults, drives and safe working

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is L1's peaks to earth climbing from 2 to 4 times normal, as each strike leaves the star point held further out, when you tap Strike with No losses, but not with Heavy losses.
interactive.title: The restrike ladder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve small screens share one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and seven ask you to try it.

A picker above the picture, View, offers three cards: Arc ladder, Drive on IT and Touch. Its buttons wrap on a phone.

Arc ladder. A sketch shows L1 of a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, one capacitor to the hull for the whole system's capacitance, and an arc gap at a chafed cable. A plot shows L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with a dashed line for the star point's. Thin guide lines mark ±359 V, L1's normal peak, and ±622 V, labelled Solid fault. The vertical scale runs to ±2,400 V. Under it are Strike, Reset and a picker, Losses: No losses, Some losses and Heavy losses, wrapping on a phone. Each tap of Strike waits for L1's next peak, then flashes the gap. After three strikes, Strike greys out until Reset. Readout tiles wrap on a phone: Star point held at, in volts; L1's highest peak, in volts; and Times normal peak.

Drive on IT. A 440 V insulated board feeds a cable of 1 µF a line and ten drives. Each drive's EMC filter is three small capacitors to the hull, 0.1 µF a line. A switch, Filters, sets them In or Out. Out, the capacitors are drawn unhooked, and a tag turns red: EMC standard not met. An insulation monitor's dial sits on the board. A picker, Monitor, offers Plain DC and Made for drives. Readout tiles wrap on a phone: First-fault current, in milliamps, and Settling time, against the cable alone.

Touch. Lines L1 to L3 run above the hull. A person stands on the hull with one hand on a line. A picker, Fault on L1, offers None and Solid. A picker, Touching, offers L1 and L2. A bar shows the voltage across the person, with a tick at 50 V marked Safe touch. Readout tiles wrap on a phone: Across you, in volts, and Through a 1,000 Ω body, in milliamps.

The rule for the ladder. Each line's normal voltage to earth is 440 ÷ 1.732 = 254 V, with a peak of 254 × 1.414 = 359 V, called 1 times. L1's voltage to the hull is the star point's held voltage plus L1's swing of 359 V either side. The first strike burns until a current zero at L1's peak, leaving the star point held 1 times out, opposite L1's swing. Each later strike comes at L1's peak, P times out. The star point jumps P across, then rings past by a share of that jump: all of it with No losses, half with Some and none with Heavy. The arc goes out at the top of the ring. So the new held voltage is (1 + ring share) × P minus the old one, and L1's next peak is that plus 1.

No losses: held 1, 3, 5 times (359, 1,077, 1,795 V), peaks 2, 4, 6 times (718, 1,436, 2,154 V). Some losses: held 1, 2, 2.5 times (359, 718, 898 V), peaks 2, 3, 3.5 times (718, 1,077, 1,257 V), heading towards 4 times. Heavy losses: held 1 times, every peak 2 times, 718 V. The ring is a short wiggle on the dashed line, slowed and enlarged.

The rule for the drives. A solid first fault passes 3 × ω × C × 254 V, with ω = 2π × 60 = 377 and C the capacitance a line: 287 mA for each µF a line. The cable's 1 µF gives 287 mA. Filters In add 10 × 0.1 = 1 µF, making 2 µF and 575 mA. Settling time grows in step with the capacitance: ×1 Out, ×2 In. With Monitor on Plain DC, the needle shakes and a tag reads: DC from the drive can upset this reading. No value is shown. With Made for drives, it is steady.

The rule for touch. Healthy, each line sits 254 V from the hull. The body current returns through all three lines' capacitance in parallel, 3 µF, or 884 Ω at 60 Hz: 254 ÷ √(1,000² + 884²) = 190 mA. With a solid fault on L1, the hull sits at L1. Touching L1 gives 0 V and 0 mA. Touching L2 gives 440 V, and the fault is a solid path back, so 440 ÷ 1,000 = 440 mA.

The opening setting is View Arc ladder, No losses, no strikes. The trace swings 359 V either side of a dashed line at 0 V.

Screen 1, show. View Arc ladder, No losses, Strike tapped once. The words: "An arcing fault strikes, goes out and strikes again. Say a chafed L1 cable arcs to the hull at L1's peak. While the arc burns, it is a solid fault, so the triangle shifts. The arc carries the system's charging current. It leads the voltage by 90°, so it is zero when the voltage peaks. The arc goes out there.[^6] At that moment the star point is a full peak, 359 V, from the hull. The charge has no quick way off, so it stays held there." Read: "The arc struck once at L1's peak and went out at a current zero. The dashed line shows the star point held 359 V from the hull." Still: one strike, run on one cycle.

Screen 2, try it. "The arc has just gone out at a current zero. What does the star point's voltage to the hull do now?" Three choices, in this order: "It falls back to 0 V, as the fault has gone"; "It stays near 359 V, held by the charge on the capacitance"; "It swings at 60 Hz about the hull, as before the fault". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Something must carry the charge away. With the arc out, there is no quick path." Hint for the third: "The capacitance now holds a charge, and the arc that put it there has gone." Why: "The arc went out as the capacitance reached its peak. The charge has no quick way off, only slow leakage. So the star point stays near 359 V, and L1 swings about it." The picture stays on one strike. Read: the question.

Screen 3, show. View Arc ladder, No losses, Strike tapped again at the next peak. The words: "L1 still swings 359 V either side of the star point. Half a cycle on, it is 718 V from the hull, twice its normal peak. Then the gap restrikes. To pull L1 to the hull, the star point must jump 718 V. That jump is sudden, so the capacitance and the supply's inductance ring, like a struck bell. With no losses, the star point rings past by as much again. The arc goes out at the top of the ring. Then L1 peaks at 4 times normal.[^10]" Read: "With no losses and two strikes, L1 peaks at 718 V, then 1,436 V. The star point is held at 359 V, then 1,077 V." Still: No losses, two strikes, run on to the next peak.

Screen 4, try it. "No losses. After the second strike, the star point is held at 1,077 V, three times the normal peak of 359 V. How high does L1 peak half a cycle later?" Three choices, in this order: "1,077 V, the voltage the star point holds"; "1,436 V, the held voltage plus L1's own swing"; "718 V, twice the normal peak". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "L1 swings 359 V either side of the star point. Add that swing." Hint for the third: "That was the first rung. The star point is now three times as far out." Why: "L1's far peak is 1,077 + 359 = 1,436 V, 4 times normal. With no losses the climb goes on until a weak part, such as a starter coil or motor winding, fails.[^11]" A right Check strikes a third time: L1 peaks at 2,154 V and Strike greys out. Read: the question.

Screen 5, show. View Arc ladder, Some losses, three strikes. The words: "Losses damp the ring. The insulation loses a little energy each time it charges, and the ring charges it thousands of times a second. With Some losses, the star point rings past by half the jump. The peaks go 2, 3, then 3.5 times normal, and level off. Ships' cables lose far more at these frequencies.[^12] So it is argued whether the climb happens at sea at all. Cases on 480 V systems have reached 1,200 V to earth.[^1]" Read: "With Some losses and three strikes, L1 peaks at 718 V, 1,077 V, then 1,257 V. The climb is levelling off." Still: Some losses, three strikes.

Screen 6, try it. "Heavy losses damp the ring completely, so the star point never rings past. The arc restrikes at every peak. How high does L1 get?" Three choices, in this order: "359 V, its normal peak, as the losses stop any rise"; "718 V, twice its normal peak, and no higher"; "It still climbs, only more slowly". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The first strike still leaves the star point held 359 V out. L1 swings past it." Hint for the third: "With no overshoot, each restrike lands the star point 359 V out on the other side." Why: "The first strike holds the star point 359 V out, so L1 reaches 718 V. Each restrike only flips it to 359 V on the other side. That is a little above the 622 V peak a solid fault puts on the healthy lines." A right Check sets Heavy losses and strikes three times: every peak is 718 V. Read: the question.

Screen 7, show. View Drive on IT, Made for drives, Filters from In to Out. The words: "A drive's EMC filter has capacitors from each line to the hull. On an insulated supply, they tie the system to earth.[^4] Ten drives at 0.1 µF a line add 1 µF a line to the cable's 1 µF. That doubles the capacitance. A solid first fault passes 575 mA, not 287 mA. The monitor takes twice as long to settle. So on an insulated supply you disconnect each filter and its varistor.[^14] The price is that the drive may no longer meet its EMC standard.[^15]" Read: "With the filters in, a solid first fault passes 575 mA and the monitor settles twice as slowly. With them out, it passes 287 mA, and the EMC tag is red." Still: Drive on IT, Filters Out, Made for drives.

Screen 8, try it. "A new drive's filter is out, as it should be on an insulated supply. Yet the monitor's reading jumps about whenever the drive runs. What do you check first?" Three choices, in this order: "Put the filter back in to steady the reading"; "That the monitor is made for supplies that feed drives"; "Nothing, as a monitor cannot see through a drive". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The filter ties the supply to the hull. That is why it came out." Hint for the third: "The monitor reads everything joined to the supply, including the drive's DC side." Why: "A drive's rectifier joins its DC side to the supply. DC leaking from there distorts a plain monitor's reading.[^17] So use a monitor made for non-linear loads.[^16]" The picture shows Drive on IT, Filters Out, Plain DC, the needle shaking. A right Check sets Made for drives. Read: the question.

Screen 9, show. View Touch, Fault on L1 Solid, Touching L2. The words: "A monitor in alarm means a line may already be joined to the hull. Then the system behaves exactly like an earthed one.[^5] Here a solid fault holds the hull at L1. Touch L2 with your feet on the hull, and you hold the full 440 V. Through a 1,000 Ω body that drives about 440 mA. Only a touch voltage below 50 V AC is counted safe.[^22] Floating is not the same as safe." Read: "With a solid fault on L1, a person on the hull touching L2 holds 440 V. About 440 mA flows through a 1,000 Ω body." Still: Touch, Fault on L1 Solid, Touching L2.

Screen 10, try it, the first of three mixed puzzles. "The monitor reads 2 MΩ, with no alarm. The cables have 1 µF a line. You stand on the hull and touch L1. What flows through a 1,000 Ω body?" Three choices, in this order: "Next to nothing, as no fault completes the circuit"; "About 190 mA, back through the cables' capacitance"; "About 440 mA, with the full line voltage across you". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Every cable is a capacitor to the hull you stand on, a path for AC." Hint for the third: "With no fault, L1 sits only 254 V from the hull, and the capacitance limits the current." Why: "The monitor reads resistance with DC, so it ignores the capacitance. But the capacitance passes AC and closes the loop through you: about 190 mA. A healthy reading is no reason to touch." A right Check sets Touch, Fault None, Touching L1. Read: the question.

Screen 11, try it. "One side says an arcing fault can pump an insulated supply's voltage up. The other says this is not a problem on ships. What does each case rest on?" Three choices, in this order: "The first on voltages measured on 480 V systems, the second on ships' heavier losses"; "The first on theory alone, the second on measurements at sea"; "Both on the same measurements, read differently". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "The 1,200 V readings were measured. The marine case rests on how hard ships damp the ring." Hint for the third: "One side measured voltages on 480 V systems. The other worked out how hard marine losses damp the ring." Why: "Voltages of 1,200 V or more were measured on 480 V systems.[^1] The marine case is that ships' heavy losses damp the ring.[^3] On the picker, light losses let the ladder climb and heavy losses stop it. Where a real ship sits is still argued." A right Check shows Arc ladder, three strikes, on No losses then Heavy losses. Read: the question.

Screen 12, try it. "You disconnect a drive's EMC filter so it suits an insulated supply. What have you given up?" Three choices, in this order: "Nothing, as the filter matters only on earthed supplies"; "Its full EMC performance, so more switching noise can reach nearby equipment"; "The drive's protection against earth faults". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The filter keeps the drive's high-frequency noise in, on any supply." Hint for the third: "The filter is there for interference, not for earth-fault protection." Why: "Without the filter, the drive may no longer meet its EMC standard.[^15] You trade that for a supply that stays floating, with less capacitance to the hull." A right Check sets Drive on IT, Filters Out, the EMC tag red. Read: the question.

Every figure here is an example value, a published figure, or worked from the rules above.
interactive.ignores: The ladder treats the whole system's capacitance as one capacitor and the supply as a steady 60 Hz source. It strikes the arc exactly at each peak, and takes the first strike to burn until a current zero with no ring. Real arcs are less regular, and fuller models of the arc give different figures. The ring is drawn slowed and enlarged: a real one runs at kilohertz and is over in well under a millisecond. The held charge is drawn as steady between strikes, though leakage slowly drains it. L2 and L3 are left out of the ladder, though they move with the star point too. On the drive card, each filter is drawn as capacitors alone, without its varistor or resistors, and the settling time follows the capacitance alone. On the touch card, the body is a fixed 1,000 Ω, and footwear, gloves and contact resistance are left out.

explain.text:
On an insulated supply, an earth fault that arcs can be worse than a solid one. Each time the arc goes out, it leaves charge on the system's capacitance. The next swing starts from that charge, so the voltage to earth can climb in steps. Losses in the cables damp the climb. How far it goes on ships is argued.

Picture a chafed L1 cable arcing to the hull. While the arc burns, it is a solid fault, so the triangle shifts. The arc carries the system's charging current. That current leads the voltage by 90°, so it passes through zero at a voltage peak. The arc goes out there, at the current zero.[^6] At that moment the shifted star point is a full peak from the hull. The charge has no quick way off, so the star point stays held there. On a 440 V supply each line's normal peak to earth is 254 × 1.414 = 359 V. L1 keeps swinging 359 V either side of the held star point. Half a cycle later it is 718 V from the hull, twice its normal peak. Then the gap restrikes. To pull L1 to the hull, the star point must jump 718 V. The jump is sudden, so the capacitance and the supply's inductance ring like a struck bell. With no losses, the ring carries the star point past by as much again, to 1,077 V. The arc goes out at the top of the ring and leaves it held there. L1 then peaks at 1,077 + 359 = 1,436 V, four times normal.[^10] Without losses, the climb goes on until a weak part fails.[^11]

Losses shrink the ring. The insulation loses a little energy each time it charges, and the ring charges it thousands of times a second. With half the ring left, the peaks go 2, 3, then 3.5 times normal and level off. With the ring fully damped, L1 stops at twice normal. Engineers have documented motors failing across whole 480 V systems while a fault was hunted.[^2] Voltages of 1,200 V or more to earth were measured in those cases.[^1] Marine engineers argue that ships' higher losses damp the ring so heavily that this is not a problem at sea.[^3] Which end of that range a ship sits at is still argued. The ladder here is a simplified model, with one capacitance and an arc that restrikes exactly at each peak.

Two more dangers come with every insulated supply. A drive's EMC filter puts capacitors from each line to the hull, tying the supply to earth.[^4] Like any capacitance, that raises the first-fault current and slows the monitor. So you disconnect it, and the drive may then no longer meet its EMC standard. And a floating supply is not safe to touch. With a first fault on one line, the system behaves exactly like an earthed one.[^5] A solid fault on L1 leaves L2 and L3 sitting 440 V from the hull. So once nothing trips, the danger is the voltage to earth: an arc may pump it up, and a touch or a second fault turns it into current. **An arc that keeps restriking can leave charge on an insulated system's capacitance and lift its voltage to earth step by step, unless losses damp the ring.[^7]**

analogy.text: Think of the reservoir capacitor behind a rectifier diode. It charges to the peak, and the diode stops it giving the charge back. The arc acts like that diode. It conducts, then goes out at a current zero, just as the capacitance reaches its peak. So the capacitance is left holding the peak, and the supply keeps swinging on top of it. That is how the voltage to earth reaches twice the normal peak.
analogy.breaks: A diode conducts the same way round every cycle, so the charge never builds past the peak. An arc restrikes whichever way the gap breaks down, and each sudden restrike rings. That ring is what can push the held charge beyond the peak, rung by rung. A reservoir also feeds a load that drains it, while here only slow leakage does.

practice.text:
- Safety first. Treat an insulated supply as live and able to kill. An alarm can mean one line is already joined to the hull, and then the system behaves like an earthed one.[^5]
- Work dead wherever possible.[^19] Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch a conductor.
- A touch voltage is counted safe only below 50 V AC.[^22] Each line of a healthy 440 V insulated supply sits about 254 V from the hull.
- Clear an earth fault that comes and goes as soon as you can. If it is arcing, each restrike may lift the voltage to earth.
- Before you connect a drive to an insulated supply, check it suits one. Disconnect its EMC filter and ground-to-phase varistor as its manual shows.[^14]
- Expect that drive may miss its EMC standard once the filter is out.[^15]
- Use an insulation monitor made for supplies with non-linear loads such as drives.[^16]
- Expect the monitor to settle more slowly as drives and cable add capacitance.

**Rule of thumb:** An insulated supply is floating, not dead. Its voltage to earth is what hurts you, and an arc can raise it.

**Worked example:** On a 440 V supply, each line's normal peak to earth is 254 × 1.414 = 359 V. A solid first fault lifts the healthy lines to 440 V, a peak of 622 V. Equipment on an insulated system is rated for that.[^23] An arc that goes out at a peak leaves the star point held 359 V away, so L1's next peak is 718 V. With no losses, the next restrike holds the star point at 1,077 V, and L1 peaks at 1,436 V. With heavy losses, L1 stays at 718 V.

**High voltage:** Ships' HV systems are usually earthed through a resistor. It limits a fault to a few amps and avoids the overvoltages a fully insulated HV system can build.[^21]

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking a floating supply is safe to touch.
- Taking a healthy monitor reading as proof a line is safe to touch. The capacitance still carries current through you.
- Putting a drive's EMC filter back in to steady an insulation monitor.
- Leaving an earth fault that comes and goes because nothing tripped.
- Treating the arcing climb as settled, either way.
